theoryAdd.text: Why is a MUX of half the size enough for an n-variable function? Shannon's expansion splits any function about one variable: F equals x̄ times F with x = 0, plus x times F with x = 1. Applying it to all the select variables shows that each data input only has to supply what is left of F for its select code, called the residue. When exactly one variable is left over, the residue is a function of that single variable, and there are only four of those: 0, 1, x and x̄.

theoryAdd.plainText: Shannon expansion: F = A' F(0,B,C) + A F(1,B,C)

theoryAdd.text: Which minterms a data input covers depends on which variable is left free. If the free variable is the least significant one, data input I_k covers the pair of minterms 2k and 2k + 1. If the free variable is the most significant one of an n-variable function, I_k covers minterms k and k + 2^(n−1), and the usual implementation table has two rows (free variable 0 and 1) and one column per data input. Any variable may be chosen as the free one; each choice gives a different but equally valid set of connections.

Example 1: F(A,B,C,D) = Σm(0,1,3,4,8,9,15) on an 8:1 MUX
S2 S1 S0 = A B C, D is free (LSB), I_k covers m(2k), m(2k+1)
I0: m0, m1    both in F        -> 1
I1: m2, m3    only m3 (D = 1)  -> D
I2: m4, m5    only m4 (D = 0)  -> D̄
I3: m6, m7    neither          -> 0
I4: m8, m9    both             -> 1
I5: m10, m11  neither          -> 0
I6: m12, m13  neither          -> 0
I7: m14, m15  only m15 (D = 1) -> D

Example 2: F(A,B,C) = Σm(0,2,3,6) on a 4:1 MUX, S1 S0 = B C, A free (MSB)
            I0    I1    I2    I3
A = 0 row   m0    m1    m2    m3
A = 1 row   m4    m5    m6    m7
in F        m0    none  m2,m6 m3
data input  Ā     0     1     Ā
Check: A B C = 1 1 0 selects I2 = 1, and m6 is in F.

Enable inputs give a second way to expand a MUX. Two 8:1 MUXes with active-low strobes, one strobed by S3 and the other by S̄3, form a 16:1 MUX when their outputs are ORed, because a disabled 74151 drives Y to 0. In a pure tree of 2:1 MUXes every block removes exactly one candidate input, so a 2^n:1 selector needs 2^n − 1 of them.

theoryAdd.plainText: Number of 2:1 MUXes for a 2^n:1 MUX = 2^n − 1 (e.g. 7 for 8:1, 31 for 32:1)

theoryAdd.text: A single 2:1 MUX with S = A works as any basic gate, which is why it is functionally complete when 0 and 1 are available:
items: A ⊕ B: I0 = B, I1 = B̄; swapping them gives A ⊙ B.
Pairing minterms 2k and 2k + 1 when the free variable is actually the MSB (the pairs are then k and k + 2^(n−1)).
Swapping x and x̄: the input gets x when only the minterm with x = 1 is in F.
Reading the select code with S0 as the most significant bit.
Assuming a disabled MUX goes to high impedance; the 74151 forces Y = 0, and only three-state parts such as the 74251 float.
Counting tree blocks by dividing only once; each stage divides again until one block remains.

theoryAdd.text: To check a MUX design quickly, pick two or three input combinations, work out which data input each one selects, and confirm that the value on that input matches the truth table.

questions.questionText: A multiplexer is best described as a circuit that:
options: Sends one input to one of several outputs
Converts a single active input line into a binary code
Selects one of several inputs and passes it to a single output
Stores one bit of data until the next clock edge
questions.explanation: A multiplexer is a data selector: the select code decides which one of the data inputs appears at the single output. Routing one input to many outputs is a demultiplexer, and coding an active line is an encoder.

questions.questionText: A demultiplexer has 4 select lines. How many output lines does it have?
questions.explanation: A DEMUX with n select lines has 2^n outputs: 2^4 = 16.

questions.questionText: In a 4:1 multiplexer, the select lines are S1 S0 = 10. Which data input is connected to the output?
questions.explanation: The select lines form a binary number with S1 as the MSB: 10₂ = 2, so I2 is selected. Reading S0 as the MSB would wrongly give I1.

questions.questionText: A 1:4 demultiplexer has data input D = 1 and select lines S1 S0 = 11. The outputs Y3 Y2 Y1 Y0 are:
questions.explanation: The data is routed only to the output selected by S1 S0 = 11₂ = 3, so Y3 = D = 1 and the other outputs stay 0: Y3 Y2 Y1 Y0 = 1000.

questions.questionText: A 1:4 demultiplexer has data input D = 0 and select lines S1 S0 = 01. The outputs Y3 Y2 Y1 Y0 are:
questions.explanation: The selected output Y1 carries the data value D = 0 and all unselected outputs are 0, so every output is 0. Y1 = 1 would only appear if D = 1.

questions.questionText: Which of the following ICs is an 8-to-1 multiplexer?
questions.explanation: The 74151 is the 8:1 data selector with outputs Y and W. The 74138 is a 3-to-8 decoder, the 74148 an 8-to-3 priority encoder and the 74157 a quad 2:1 MUX.

questions.questionText: The 74153 IC contains:
options: Four 2:1 multiplexers that share one select line
One 8:1 multiplexer with true and complemented outputs
Two 4:1 multiplexers that share the same select lines
questions.explanation: The 74153 is a dual 4-line-to-1-line data selector: both halves use the common select inputs A and B but have separate active-low strobes. Four 2:1 MUXes is the 74157 and the 8:1 with Y and W is the 74151.

questions.questionText: The active-low strobe (enable) input of a 74151 8:1 multiplexer is held HIGH. The output Y:
options: Holds the value of the last selected input
Is forced to 0 regardless of the select and data inputs
questions.explanation: When the strobe is inactive the 74151 disables its AND gates, so Y = 0 and W = 1 whatever the other inputs are. It has no memory, and only three-state versions such as the 74251 float their outputs.

questions.questionText: A 2:1 multiplexer has select S = A, data inputs I0 = B and I1 = B̄. The output Y equals:
questions.explanation: Y = S̄·I0 + S·I1 = ĀB + AB̄, which is the exclusive-OR A ⊕ B.

questions.questionText: To make a 2:1 multiplexer act as an inverter for the variable A, the connections should be:
questions.explanation: Y = Ā·I0 + A·I1 = Ā·1 + A·0 = Ā. With I0 = 0 and I1 = 1 the MUX is only a buffer (Y = A), and the other two give a constant 0.

questions.questionText: A 2:1 multiplexer has select S = A, I0 = B and I1 = 1. Its output is:
questions.explanation: Y = Ā·B + A·1 = ĀB + A = A + B (absorption). The circuit therefore acts as a 2-input OR gate.

questions.questionText: F(A,B,C) = Σm(0,2,5,7) is implemented on a 4:1 MUX with A on S1, B on S0 and C used at the data inputs. The data inputs I0, I1, I2, I3 are:
questions.explanation: I0 covers m0, m1 (only m0, C = 0) → C̄; I1 covers m2, m3 (only m2) → C̄; I2 covers m4, m5 (only m5, C = 1) → C; I3 covers m6, m7 (only m7) → C.

questions.questionText: F(A,B,C,D) = Σm(1,3,4,11,12,13,14,15) is implemented on an 8:1 MUX with A, B, C on S2, S1, S0 and D applied to the data inputs. The data inputs I0 to I7 are:
An 8:1 MUX has A, B, C on S2, S1, S0 and data inputs I0 to I7 = 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1. The function realised is:
questions.explanation: The 1s are on I1, I2, I4, I7, so F = Σm(1,2,4,7). These are the combinations with an odd number of 1s, which is the 3-input XOR (the sum of a full adder).

questions.questionText: An 8:1 MUX with A, B, C on S2, S1, S0 has data inputs I0 to I7 = 1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0. The function is:
questions.explanation: With constants on the data inputs, F contains minterm i exactly when I_i = 1: I0, I3, I4, I5 → Σm(0,3,4,5). Σm(2,3,4,7) comes from reading the list backwards, and the other two are the complement.

questions.questionText: F(A,B,C) = Σm(1,3,5,6) is implemented on a 4:1 MUX with B on S1, C on S0, and A (the MSB) applied to the data inputs. The data inputs I0, I1, I2, I3 are:
questions.explanation: With A free, I_k covers m_k (A = 0) and m_(k+4) (A = 1): I0 (m0, m4) none → 0; I1 (m1, m5) both → 1; I2 (m2, m6) only m6 → A; I3 (m3, m7) only m3 → Ā.

questions.questionText: How many 2:1 multiplexers are needed to build a 32:1 multiplexer as a tree?
questions.explanation: The stages need 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 31 blocks, i.e. 2^n − 1 with n = 5. Every 2:1 block removes exactly one candidate input, and 32 − 1 inputs must be eliminated.

questions.questionText: A 16:1 MUX is built from two 8:1 MUXes with active-low enables (one handling I0–I7, the other I8–I15), with S2 S1 S0 common to both and their outputs ORed. The MSB select S3 should be connected to:
options: The enables of both MUXes directly
The enable of the I0–I7 MUX directly and the enable of the I8–I15 MUX through an inverter
The enable of the I0–I7 MUX through an inverter and the enable of the I8–I15 MUX directly
The S0 inputs of both MUXes
questions.explanation: For S3 = 0 the low MUX must be enabled, so its active-low enable gets S3 itself; for S3 = 1 the high MUX must be enabled, so it gets S̄3. The disabled MUX outputs 0, so the OR gate passes the selected input.

questions.questionText: How many 4:1 multiplexers are needed to build a 64:1 multiplexer?
questions.explanation: First stage 64/4 = 16 MUXes, second stage 16/4 = 4, third stage 4/4 = 1, total 21 = (64 − 1)/(4 − 1). Stopping after the first stage gives 16 and forgetting the last block gives 20.

questions.questionText: A 16:1 MUX is made of five 4:1 MUXes: first-stage MUX M0 handles I0–I3, M1 handles I4–I7, M2 handles I8–I11 and M3 handles I12–I15, and all first-stage MUXes use S1 S0. For S3 S2 S1 S0 = 1110, the output comes from:
questions.explanation: S1 S0 = 10 makes every first-stage MUX pass its input 2, and S3 S2 = 11 makes the second stage choose M3, so I(4·3 + 2) = I14 appears; 1110₂ = 14 confirms it.

questions.questionText: Which of the following is NOT a typical application of a multiplexer?
options: Storing a data bit between clock pulses
Implementing a Boolean function without simplification
Selecting one of several data sources for a bus
questions.explanation: A MUX is purely combinational and has no memory, so it cannot store data; that needs a latch or flip-flop. The other three are standard MUX applications.

questions.questionText: A 3-bit up-counter (000 → 111) drives the select lines of an 8:1 MUX whose inputs are I0 to I7 = 1, 1, 0, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0. The serial bit sequence at the output over eight clock pulses, first bit first, is:
questions.explanation: The counter selects I0, I1, … I7 in turn, so the inputs appear in order: 1 1 0 1 0 0 1 0. Reading from I7 down gives the reversed pattern 01001011.

questions.questionText: A 4:1 MUX has S1 = A, S0 = B and data inputs I0 = 0, I1 = C, I2 = C, I3 = 1. The output is:
questions.explanation: F = ĀB̄·0 + ĀB·C + AB̄·C + AB·1 = Σm(3,5,6,7), which is 1 when at least two inputs are 1: the majority function AB + BC + CA.

questions.questionText: The carry output of a full adder is implemented on a 4:1 MUX with A on S1, B on S0 and Cin at the data inputs. The data inputs I0, I1, I2, I3 are:
questions.explanation: Carry = Σm(3,5,6,7). AB = 00 gives no carry → 0; AB = 01 and 10 give a carry only when Cin = 1 → Cin; AB = 11 always carries → 1. The pattern Cin, C̄in, C̄in, Cin is the sum output.

questions.questionText: The borrow output of a full subtractor (X − Y − Bin) is implemented on a 4:1 MUX with X on S1, Y on S0 and Bin at the data inputs. The data inputs I0, I1, I2, I3 are:
questions.explanation: Bout = X̄Y + X̄·Bin + Y·Bin = Σm(1,2,3,7). XY = 00 borrows only if Bin = 1 → Bin; XY = 01 always borrows → 1; XY = 10 never → 0; XY = 11 only if Bin = 1 → Bin.

questions.questionText: A 1:8 demultiplexer can be used as a 3-to-8 line decoder by:
options: Holding its data input at logic 0 and applying the code to the select lines
Holding its data input at logic 1 and applying the 3-bit code to the select lines
Applying the code to the data input and grounding the select lines
Feeding the outputs back to the select lines
questions.explanation: With D = 1 the selected output becomes 1 and all others 0, which is exactly the decoder behaviour D_i = m_i(S). With D = 0 every output would stay 0.

questions.questionText: A 1:16 demultiplexer is built from five 1:4 demultiplexers so that second-stage DEMUX k drives outputs Y(4k) to Y(4k+3). The first-stage DEMUX, which receives the data, must be driven by:
options: The two least significant select bits S1 S0
All four select bits S3 to S0
The two most significant select bits S3 S2
questions.explanation: The first stage chooses which group of four outputs gets the data, and the group number k is given by S3 S2. Each second-stage DEMUX then uses S1 S0 to pick one output within its group.

questions.questionText: A multiplexer at the transmitting end and a demultiplexer at the receiving end, driven by the same select code, allow:
options: Data to be stored for later use
Parallel data to be converted to Gray code
Several signals to share a single transmission line in turn
questions.explanation: This is time-division multiplexing: the MUX puts each source on the shared line in its time slot and the DEMUX, using the same select code, delivers it to the matching destination.

questions.questionText: Which of the following statements about multiplexers is NOT correct?
options: A MUX with n select lines has 2^n data inputs
A 4:1 MUX can realise every 4-variable function with only 0 and 1 on its data inputs
A 2^n:1 MUX can realise any n-variable function with no extra gates
A 2^(n−1):1 MUX can realise any n-variable function if one variable and its complement are available
questions.explanation: A 4:1 MUX has only two select lines, so with constant data inputs it can realise functions of just two variables; for four variables it needs functions of the other two variables on its data inputs. The other statements are standard results.

questions.questionText: The method of implementing an n-variable function on a 2^(n−1):1 multiplexer, with one variable at the data inputs, is based on:
questions.explanation: Shannon's expansion F = x̄·F(x = 0) + x·F(x = 1) splits the function into residues for each select code; with one variable left, each residue is 0, 1, x or x̄.

questions.questionText: F(A,B,C,D) = Σm(0,2,5,7,8,9,13,15) is implemented on an 8:1 MUX with B, C, D on S2, S1, S0 and A (the MSB) at the data inputs. The data inputs I0 to I7 are:
questions.explanation: With A free, I_k covers m_k and m_(k+8): (0,8) both → 1; (1,9) only 9 → A; (2,10) only 2 → Ā; (3,11) and (4,12) none → 0; (5,13) both → 1; (6,14) none → 0; (7,15) both → 1.

questions.questionText: When a 4-variable function is implemented on an 8:1 MUX with three variables on the select lines, each data input is connected to:
options: Any function of two of the variables
0, 1, the fourth variable or its complement
questions.explanation: Each data input covers two minterms that differ only in the fourth variable, so its residue can only be 0, 1, that variable or its complement.

questions.questionText: F(A,B,C,D) = Σm(0,1,2,3,5,7,10,12,13,14,15) is implemented on a 4:1 MUX with A on S1 and B on S0. The data inputs I0, I1, I2, I3 must be:
questions.explanation: AB = 00 covers m0–m3, all in F → 1; AB = 01 covers m4–m7, only m5 and m7 (D = 1) → D; AB = 10 covers m8–m11, only m10 (CD = 10) → CD̄; AB = 11 covers m12–m15, all → 1.

questions.questionText: A 4:1 MUX has S1 = A, S0 = B and data inputs I0 = C, I1 = 0, I2 = 1, I3 = C̄. The function in minterm form is:
questions.explanation: I0 = C gives m1 (ABC = 001); I1 = 0 gives nothing; I2 = 1 gives m4 and m5; I3 = C̄ gives m6 (110). So F = Σm(1,4,5,6).

questions.questionText: Another name for a multiplexer is:
questions.explanation: A multiplexer selects one of many inputs, hence data selector. Data distributor is the usual name for a demultiplexer.

questions.questionText: An 8:1 multiplexer without an enable input is built in two-level form from basic gates. It needs:
options: Eight 4-input AND gates, one 8-input OR gate and inverters for the select lines
Eight 3-input AND gates, one 8-input OR gate and inverters for the select lines
Three 8-input AND gates and one 3-input OR gate
Eight 4-input OR gates and one 8-input AND gate
questions.explanation: Each data input needs an AND gate combining the three select literals with the data bit (3 + 1 = 4 inputs), and one 8-input OR gate collects the eight products. Forgetting the data input gives the 3-input answer.

questions.questionText: In a 1:4 demultiplexer with data input D and select lines S1 S0, the output Y2 equals:
questions.explanation: Y2 is selected by S1 S0 = 10, so Y2 = D·m2 = D·S1·S̄0. Leaving out D gives a decoder output, not a demultiplexer output.

questions.questionText: Two 4-bit data sources must share one 4-bit bus, with one control line choosing the source. The most suitable single IC is:
options: A quad 2:1 multiplexer such as the 74157
questions.explanation: Each of the four bus bits needs its own 2:1 selector, and the 74157 has four 2:1 MUXes sharing one select line, so one control bit switches all four bits together.

questions.questionText: An 8:1 MUX driven by a 3-bit counter converts a byte to serial form. The counter is clocked at 2 MHz, one bit per clock. How long does it take to send one byte?
questions.explanation: Each bit lasts one clock period T = 1/2 MHz = 0.5 µs, and a byte needs 8 bits: 8 × 0.5 µs = 4 µs. Using the 3 select bits instead of 8 data bits gives 1.5 µs.

questions.questionText: A 3-bit counter (000 → 111, repeating) clocked at 80 kHz drives the selects of an 8:1 MUX whose inputs I0 to I7 = 1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0. The output is a square wave of frequency:
questions.explanation: The pattern repeats every 8 clocks (four 1s then four 0s), so one output period is 8 clock periods: f = 80 kHz / 8 = 10 kHz, with 50% duty cycle.

questions.questionText: A 74151 8:1 MUX (outputs Y and W = Ȳ) is programmed on its data inputs for F(A,B,C) = Σm(2,3,5). The W output realises:
questions.explanation: W is the complement of Y, so it is 1 for every minterm not in F: Σm(0,1,4,6,7). Note that ΠM(0,1,4,6,7) is the same as Σm(2,3,5), which is Y.

questions.questionText: MUX 1 (2:1) has S = A, I0 = B, I1 = C. Its output M1 feeds I0 of MUX 2 (2:1), which has S = B and I1 = A. The output of MUX 2 is:
questions.explanation: M1 = ĀB + AC. MUX 2 gives Y = B̄·M1 + B·A = B̄(ĀB + AC) + AB = AB̄C + AB = A(B + C) = AB + AC.

questions.questionText: What is the minimum number of select lines needed for a multiplexer that must choose one of 12 data inputs?
questions.explanation: n must satisfy 2^n ≥ 12; 2^3 = 8 is too few and 2^4 = 16 is enough, so 4 select lines are needed (four of the 16 codes are unused).

questions.questionText: F(A,B,C) = A + BC is implemented on an 8:1 MUX with A, B, C on S2, S1, S0 and constants on the data inputs. How many data inputs are tied to logic 1?
questions.explanation: A = 1 gives m4 to m7 and BC = 11 gives m3 and m7. The union is {3, 4, 5, 6, 7}, 5 minterms; counting m7 twice gives 6.

questions.questionText: A 4:1 MUX has S1 = A, S0 = B and data inputs I0 = C, I1 = 1, I2 = C, I3 = 0. The minimal SOP form of its output is:
questions.explanation: The output is Σm(1,2,3,5): I0 = C gives m1, I1 = 1 gives m2 and m3, I2 = C gives m5. Grouping gives ĀB (m2, m3) and B̄C (m1, m5).

questions.questionText: When a 3-variable function is implemented on a 4:1 MUX, the variable applied to the data inputs:
options: Must always be the most significant variable
Must always be the least significant variable
Must be the variable that appears in the most minterms
May be any one of the three; each choice gives a valid but different set of data-input connections
questions.explanation: Shannon's expansion works about any variable, so any one can be left free; only the pairing of minterms and hence the data-input values change with the choice.
